definition: Stratification means the arrangement of people or things into distinct, ranked layers or levels.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word stratification. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know stratification should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Beneath the polite dinner conversation lay a rigid stratification, in which the seating itself announced who stood above whom.
A mixed crowd has no order at all, while stratification locks everyone into distinct layers ranked one above another.
Grouped items sit in separate but equal categories; stratification goes further by stacking those groups into higher and lower ranks.

A hierarchy is a system of ranked levels of authority — who stands over whom and who answers to whom. Stratification emphasizes the layered separation of a whole population into levels: not the chain of command itself, but the way an entire society settles into ranked bands.

A ranking orders individual items along a single scale, first to last, like a league table. Stratification gathers many members into distinct layers or bands at similar levels — whole classes rather than single positions — and stacks those layers by status.

Layering captures the level-upon-level structure, but it can be purely physical and neutral — layering rock, layering clothes. Stratification adds rank: its layers stand higher and lower in status, not merely one atop another.
The principle that all people are equal and belong to no ranked layer; it directly opposes stratification's division of a population into higher and lower levels.
A state of being the same throughout, with no distinct layers or levels to rank — where stratification stacks differences, uniformity erases them.

On the naval vessel, stratification divided the crew into sharply ranked layers, with senior officers berthed on the upper decks, petty officers just below them, and enlisted sailors packed into the cramped lower quarters near the hull.
Stratification means arrangement into distinct, ranked layers stacked one above another by status or level.

It is not just any grouping or sorting (you can separate people into equal categories that have no top and no bottom); stratification specifically requires layers that sit above and below one another in a fixed order of rank.
The crew split across higher and lower decks strictly by rank is the definition of stratification.
Stratification is the precise term for arrangement into ranked layers, especially in sociology, geology, and ecology.
In everyday speech, say 'the class system,' 'levels,' or 'pecking order,' but stratification is the exact word when you want to emphasize a whole system divided into distinct, ranked layers.

The ocean liners of 1910 were floating diagrams of their societies.
A single ship carried three sealed worlds: first class on the upper decks, second below it, steerage at the waterline -- stratification you could walk through in ten minutes of stairs.
The layers were not just physical.
Each deck had its own food, its own doctors, its own promenade, and gates kept passengers where their tickets placed them.
Historians note that the arrangement sorted whole groups rather than persons: a steerage passenger of genius still ate at the steerage table.
When reformers later attacked the design, they were attacking the idea beneath it -- that a population could be divided into bands and the bands stacked.
